title: Changing your leadership style to the situation
blurb: Explain why one leadership style never fits every person or moment, and match directing, coaching, supporting or delegating to competence, commitment and circumstances.
question: A library refurbishment project has a keen graduate planner who has never built a schedule, an experienced quantity surveyor who lost confidence after a cost overrun on her last job, and an expert site manager. Midway through, a flood shuts the site. Why should the project manager lead each of them differently, and how should her style change during the flood?

teach.body: Situational leadership (for example, Hersey and Blanchard's model) says the best style depends on the situation, above all on the follower's COMPETENCE and COMMITMENT for the task in hand. The leader varies two behaviours: directive behaviour (telling people what, how and when) and supportive behaviour (listening, encouraging and involving). In plain English: give people the amount of direction and support they actually need, and change it as they and the project change.

teach.caption: The names in brackets are the original labels (telling, selling, participating, delegating). Exams may use either set.

teach.h: Match the style to the person and task
head: The follower
Competence / commitment
Style
teach.caption: It's per TASK: the same person can be an expert at one task and a beginner at another.

steps.label: Directing
steps.sub: High direction, low support: clear steps, close checks

steps.label: Coaching
steps.sub: High direction, high support: explain why, invite ideas

steps.label: Supporting
steps.sub: Low direction, high support: listen, encourage, share decisions

steps.label: Delegating
steps.sub: Low direction, low support: agree outcomes, step back

teach.caption: Direction falls steadily; support rises then falls. If performance dips (a new task, a setback), step back to a more directive style.

teach.h: Why the style has to change
teach.body: People differ, tasks differ and projects change. Over-directing capable people causes disengagement, frustration and dependency on the PM. Under-directing novices causes confusion, errors and delay. Beyond the individual, other factors shift the right style: a crisis versus a stable phase, the team's maturity (its Tuckman stage), the organisation's culture, urgency and risk. A good PM reads the situation, chooses deliberately and keeps reassessing.

teach.caption: In iterative projects the team self-organises, so the PM mostly supports and delegates while the product owner sets priorities.

teach.body: Aisha directs the graduate planner: step-by-step guidance and regular checks while he builds his first schedule. She supports the quantity surveyor, who is skilled but shaken: she listens, asks for her view and backs her estimates. She delegates to the expert site manager: agreed outcomes and tolerances, light-touch review. When a flood shuts the site, Aisha directs everyone for 48 hours, then returns to supporting and delegating once the crisis is contained.

teach.text: Three traps. 1) Coaching is HIGH direction and HIGH support; supporting is LOW direction and HIGH support: exam options swap them. 2) Delegating is not abdicating: the leader still agrees goals and monitors outcomes. 3) Style is matched to the person ON A TASK, not fixed per person.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Say why: no one style suits every person, task or moment; the right style depends on competence and commitment.
Name the styles: directing, coaching, supporting, delegating, defined by levels of direction and support.
Match style to the scenario: identify each person's competence and commitment for THIS task.
Add situational factors: crisis vs stable phase, team maturity, culture, urgency, risk, life cycle.
Give consequences of not adapting: over-control disengages experts; under-direction confuses novices; delivery suffers.
Situational leadership: adapt style to the follower's competence and commitment for the task.
Coaching = high direction + high support; supporting = low direction + high support.
Crisis, risk, urgency, culture and team maturity also shift the right style.
Reassess continually: step back to more direction when a task is new or performance dips.

summary: You can now explain why a project manager must change leadership style with the situation, and match directing, coaching, supporting or delegating to a person's competence and commitment. You can also factor in crises, risk, culture, team maturity and the life cycle.

A.q: In situational leadership, which two factors about the follower mainly determine the style to use?
A.why: The style is matched to the follower's competence (skill and knowledge for the task) and commitment (motivation and confidence).

whyNot.0: Seniority and salary don't tell you how much direction or support someone needs on a task.
whyNot.1: Long service doesn't guarantee competence on a new task.
whyNot.2: Job titles are formal labels; the model looks at task-specific competence and commitment.

A.q: Which leadership style combines HIGH direction with HIGH support?
A.why: Coaching (selling) keeps direction high while adding high support: explaining decisions and inviting ideas.

whyNot.0: Directing is high direction with low support.
whyNot.2: Supporting is low direction with high support.
whyNot.3: Delegating is low direction with low support.

A.q: Which style BEST suits a highly skilled, self-motivated team member working on a familiar task?
A.why: High competence and high commitment call for delegating: agree the outcome and let them get on with it.

whyNot.1: Directing would over-control an expert and risk disengagement.
whyNot.2: Coaching gives more direction than a self-reliant expert needs.
whyNot.3: Telling is the original name for directing, which is too controlling here.

B.q: A new apprentice joins a rail project. She is keen but has never carried out a site survey. Which approach is MOST appropriate for that task?
options: Leave her to learn by her mistakes
B.why: Low competence with high commitment calls for directing: clear instructions, demonstration and close checks.

whyNot.0: Delegating assumes competence she doesn't yet have.
whyNot.1: Her commitment is already high; what she lacks is direction on how to do the task.
whyNot.3: Leaving a novice to fail is abdication, not a leadership style, and risks quality and safety.

B.q: Why may a project manager need to change leadership style during a project?
options: Team capability, urgency and risk change over time
Governance requires a new style at each decision gate
A single style is set by the sponsor at the start
Leadership styles expire at the end of each phase
B.why: As the team grows in competence and the project moves between stable phases and crises, the right mix of direction and support changes.

whyNot.1: Governance controls decisions and funding; it doesn't prescribe leadership styles at gates.
whyNot.2: The sponsor doesn't fix one style; the PM adapts it to the situation.
whyNot.3: Styles don't expire with phases; they change because the situation changes.

B.q: An experienced analyst is fully capable but has lost confidence after a project failure. Which style BEST fits?
options: Directing: tell her exactly what to do
Delegating: hand over and step back
B.why: High competence with variable commitment (low confidence) calls for supporting: little direction, lots of encouragement and shared decisions.

whyNot.0: She already knows how to do the work; telling her would undermine her further.
whyNot.1: Stepping right back ignores her dip in confidence.
whyNot.2: Coaching keeps direction high, which she doesn't need.

C.q: A data centre migration team has been performing well under a delegating style. A critical outage hits the live service at 2am. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep delegating; the team is in the performing stage
Take a directive lead until the crisis is contained
Call a workshop to build consensus on the next step
Escalate to the sponsor and wait for instructions
C.why: A crisis with high urgency and risk justifies a temporary, more directive style, even with a capable team. Once contained, the PM returns to delegating.

whyNot.0: Situational factors such as a crisis can override the usual style.
whyNot.2: There is no time for a consensus workshop during a live outage.
whyNot.3: The PM should lead the immediate response; escalation may follow, but waiting wastes critical time.

C.q:
Which TWO are likely results of using a directing style with a highly capable, committed team?
1. Disengagement and loss of ownership
2. Faster learning for the team
3. Dependency on the project manager
4. More creative problem-solving
C.why: Over-directing experts tends to disengage them (1) and make them wait for the PM's decisions (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is unlikely: capable people learn more from autonomy than from being told.
whyNot.1: Both 2 and 4 are unlikely; close direction stifles learning and creativity.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: over-direction reduces creative problem-solving.

C.q: A reliable developer performs well on coding but has been asked to run user testing for the first time, and is struggling. What does situational leadership suggest?
options: More direction for testing, still delegate the coding
Keep delegating everything; she is a proven performer
Switch to directing on all her tasks until she improves
Move the testing task to someone else immediately
C.why: Style is matched to the person on each task: she needs more direction on the unfamiliar testing work while coding can stay delegated.

whyNot.1: Being proven at coding doesn't make her competent at testing.
whyNot.2: Directing her coding would over-control a task she does well.
whyNot.3: Removing the task avoids developing her; the model says adjust the style, not abandon the task.

reteach.title: Think of learning to drive
reteach.question: Picture a driving instructor taking a learner from the first lesson to the day they pass. Does the instructor behave the same way every lesson?

blocks.h: The instructor changes, because the learner changes
blocks.body: Lesson one: the instructor tells the learner everything: mirror, signal, manoeuvre (directing). A few weeks in, the learner is frustrated by roundabouts, so the instructor still guides but explains why and encourages (coaching). Later the learner can drive well but is nervous on the motorway, so the instructor stays mostly quiet and reassuring (supporting). After the test, the keys are handed over (delegating).

blocks.h: From first lesson to full licence

blocks.text: Even a qualified driver needs a bit of direction the first time they tow a caravan. New task, new style.

explain.body: Directive behaviour tells people what to do, how and when, and checks it. Supportive behaviour listens, encourages, explains and involves people in decisions. Each style is a different mix of the two.

test.q: In situational leadership, what does 'supportive behaviour' mean?
options: Telling people what, how and when
test.why: Supportive behaviour builds confidence and commitment through listening, encouragement and involvement.

whyNot.0: Telling what, how and when is directive behaviour.
whyNot.1: Checking against the baseline is control, closer to directive behaviour.
whyNot.2: Approving spend is a governance and financial authority task, not a leadership behaviour.

explain.body: Directing: high direction, low support. Coaching: high direction, high support. Supporting: low direction, high support. Delegating: low direction, low support.

test.q: A PM says to a team member: 'You know how to do this. What do you think we should do? I'll back you.' Which style is this?
test.why: Little direction but plenty of encouragement and shared decision-making: that is supporting.

whyNot.0: Directing would tell the person what to do.
whyNot.1: Coaching keeps direction high; here the PM gives none.
whyNot.3: Delegating would hand over with little support; here the PM offers active backing.

explain.body: As someone's competence and commitment for a task grow, the leader moves from directing to coaching to supporting to delegating. If the task changes or performance dips, the leader moves back to a more directive style.

test.q: Which sequence shows the styles as a follower's competence and commitment grow?
test.why: Direction falls as competence grows: directing, then coaching, then supporting, then delegating.

whyNot.2: Directing comes before coaching, and supporting before delegating.
whyNot.3: Coaching (high direction) comes before supporting (low direction).

explain.body: The situation matters too. A crisis or safety-critical risk calls for more direction, even with a capable team. A stable phase, an open culture or a mature, self-organising iterative team allows more delegation.

test.q: Which factor would MOST justify a more directive style, even with a capable team?
options: A stable phase with low risk
A team at the performing stage
test.why: Emergencies with high risk and urgency need fast, clear direction whatever the team's capability.

whyNot.0: A stable, low-risk phase favours delegation.
whyNot.2: Self-organising teams call for supporting and delegating.
